clue.text: Awful telephone company's reported two types of complaint

definitions.note: The complaint is one illness; 'two types' points at the numbered forms it comes in, so the plural belongs to the description rather than to the answer.

indicators.note: What is reported has been passed on by mouth, so you want the sound of the words and not their spelling.

parts.note: dire straits are awful ones
BT is Britain's best-known telephone company
run the two pieces together and the break between them moves, leaving one medical word

explanation.walkthrough: The setter is counting on you hearing an advert for a phone network. Everything depends on saying the pieces quickly rather than looking at them.
explanation.definitionFit: two types of complaint → DIABETES: the illness is classified as type 1 and type 2, so naming the pair of types names the disease itself.

clue.text: See two tins blended in food processor

indicators.note: Blending stirs everything together until nothing is where it started, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: three letters taken exactly as they stand
a tin twice over, six more letters for the mix

explanation.walkthrough: 'Food processor' is doing double duty: on the surface it is the gadget the tins are going into, and in the definition it is a piece of you.
explanation.definitionFit: food processor → INTESTINE: the gut is where swallowed food is broken down and absorbed, so it processes food literally rather than in a kitchen.

clue.text: First in by-election ballot box, someone over-performing?

definitions.text: First in by-election ballot box, someone over-performing?
definitions.note: A semi-&lit: read straight the sentence describes a person, and read as wordplay every one of its words also hands over letters.

indicators.note: What comes first in a word is its opening letter, and none of the rest of the word is wanted.

parts.note: the letter it starts with
an urn is the vessel votes are dropped into, a standing crossword equation
an actor who over-plays a part is a ham

explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate definition to find: the sentence is the description and the wordplay at the same time, which is why every word of it also pays its way in letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue sketches the Greater Manchester mayor - a politician tipped to top any ballot on offer - while its own words also spell the surname.

clue.text: Conservative forking out nothing in tax

indicators.note: To fork out is to hand something over and be left without it, so whatever is named next leaves the word.

parts.note: the Conservative party has been the Tory party for two centuries
nothing is a zero, and a zero is written as this letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' for O is worth banking: nothing, love, duck and ring all hand you the same round letter, and a clue that wants one usually says one of the four.
explanation.definitionFit: tax → TRY: to tax a person's patience is to strain it, and that strained sense is what a trying day does to you.

clue.text: One consigned to watery grave

indicators.note: To be consigned to somewhere is to be put inside it and left there, so this letter goes into the middle of the word.

parts.note: serous fluid is the thin watery kind, the doctor's adjective for it
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: The surface buries somebody at sea. Both of the words that matter have to change part of speech: 'watery' becomes a medical adjective and 'grave' stops being a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: grave → SERIOUS: a grave illness or a grave mistake is a serious one, the adjective sense the surface hides behind the burial noun.

clue.text: Little'un runs into quiet kid causing trouble

indicators.note: Going into something means ending up inside it, so this piece drops between the letters already assembled instead of after them.

parts.note: the noise you make to hush somebody
R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for runs
a mischievous child is an imp

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket supplies the single letter: on a scorecard runs are abbreviated to R, and that convention turns up in clue after clue once you know it.
explanation.definitionFit: Little'un → SHRIMP: calling a small person a shrimp borrows the tiny crustacean's name, an affectionate put-down rather than a description.

clue.text: Cheap restaurant sold sandwiches in grand structure outside

definitions.note: The answer ends -ing but is a noun rather than a verb form: it names the erected framework itself, which is why a noun defines it.

indicators.note: A sandwich holds its filling between two outer layers, so one word opens up and takes another inside it.

parts.note: taken as it stands, and it is the word that opens up
a caff is the British greasy-spoon cafe
IN as it stands, then G, the abbreviation for grand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sold sandwiches' carries the whole surface - a cheap place selling food - while the wordplay wants 'sold' to open up and swallow the restaurant instead.
explanation.definitionFit: structure outside → SCAFFOLDING: the temporary lattice of poles and boards put up around the outside of a building while work goes on.

clue.text: Nearly all go back to church to celebrate

indicators.note: Nearly all of a word is every letter but one, and the one given up here is the last.

parts.note: to go back to a group is to rejoin it, and this arrives a letter short
CE is the Church of England

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a congregation heading home. Reading 'go back to' as one verb rather than three directions is the step that opens the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: celebrate → REJOICE: to rejoice is to show great joy openly, the celebrating that is felt and expressed rather than the kind with a cake.

clue.text: Leader during flight sees half-hearted order overturned

indicators.note: The heart of a word is its middle, and half of a doubled middle is one of the pair.
Something overturned ends up the other way up, so the assembled letters are read from the far end.

parts.note: SEES has a double E at its heart, and half a heart leaves one of them
the Order of Merit is OM after a name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' is the Exodus, not an aeroplane. OM for the Order of Merit is worth banking: a clue that says order and wants two letters usually means this one.
explanation.definitionFit: Leader during flight → MOSES: the Israelites' escape from Egypt is a flight from slavery, and the answer names the one who led it.

clue.text: Robust seat at the front, like a stool?

indicators.note: What stands at the front of a word is its opening letter, and that is all this piece contributes.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
in the medical sense a stool is a turd, so turd-like is turdy

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is warning you twice over: 'turdy' is the setter's own coinage, and 'stool' is the word a doctor uses rather than the furniture the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: Robust → STURDY: a sturdy chair or a sturdy build is solidly made and hard to knock over, which is robustness in a physical thing.

clue.text: Interpret right tune another time

parts.note: to read a situation is to interpret it
a just decision is a right one

explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are ordinary words wearing their less obvious senses - reading as interpretation, just as fairness - which is what keeps the surface looking like a note about music.
explanation.definitionFit: tune another time → READJUST: to readjust is to set something right once more, and re-tuning an instrument or a carburettor is exactly that.

clue.text: Straight bananas for sale with EC regulators' backing

indicators.note: To go bananas is to go completely to pieces, and letters in that state will not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: thirteen letters taken exactly as they stand

indicators.note: A thing's backing is what sits at its back, so the word in front of it gives up only its final letter.

parts.note: the letter at the back of the word, and the fourteenth for the mix

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the old tabloid myth about Brussels banning bendy bananas, which is why 'bananas' reads as part of the story rather than as the instruction it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Straight → AS THE CROW FLIES: the phrase measures a distance by the direct line a bird would take, ignoring the bends of any road.

clue.text: Study cape worn by model

parts.note: C. is the map-maker's abbreviation for Cape
clothes you are wearing are on you
a template is the pattern everything else is modelled on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface dresses a model in a cape. Two conventions are worth keeping from it: C for Cape on any map, and 'worn' for ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Study → CONTEMPLATE: to contemplate something is to look at it long and thoughtfully, the 'study' that means gaze at rather than revise for an exam.

clue.text: Greeting leather-clad male who might take you out?

parts.note: the shortest greeting there is

indicators.note: To be clad in a thing is to be wrapped in it, so the word before this one closes around the word after it.

parts.note: tan is leather, named for the tanning that makes it
M is the standard abbreviation for male, as on any form

explanation.walkthrough: Everything hinges on reading 'leather-clad male' as an instruction rather than a description: it is not somebody in leathers, it is one piece wrapped around another.
explanation.definitionFit: who might take you out? → HITMAN: a hitman is a contract killer, and to take someone out is gangland's polite way of saying the same thing.

clue.text: Having bucks to spare, doctor loves NYC

definitions.note: The clue describes the condition where the answer names it - a setter may swap a state for the abstract noun that labels it.

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it until it is not what it was, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: five letters taken exactly as they stand
New York City by the three initials everyone uses

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is the only word here that is neither definition nor material, and it hides by looking like the person in the story rather than the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Having bucks to spare → SOLVENCY: solvency is being able to meet every debt with money left over, and 'bucks' is the everyday word for it.

clue.text: Following date, let Neil chat nurses up?

indicators.note: To nurse a thing is to hold it close and keep it, so these words are keeping something tucked away inside them.
In a down clue 'up' means read from the bottom, so the letters run against the direction of the writing.

parts.note: start at the C of 'chat' and read backwards to the E of 'date'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a night out with Neil. A buried word running backwards is much harder to see than a forward one, so 'up' in a down clue is the flag to trust.
explanation.definitionFit: Following → CLIENTELE: a firm's clientele is the body of customers who keep coming back, which is what a following amounts to in business.

clue.text: Depression ten times, perhaps self-indulgent?

parts.note: deca- is the prefix that multiplies by ten, as in decathlon or decalitre
a depression in a car door is a dent

explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the opposite order to the clue, which is the whole difficulty here: the depression is the tail of the answer even though it opens the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: self-indulgent → DECADENT: the word has slid from moral decline to plain luxury, so a decadent pudding is simply an over-rich one.

clue.text: Con advances towards guards

indicators.note: A guard stands around whatever is being protected, so the word doing the guarding closes over the other one.

parts.note: both words point a movement in a direction
an advance in a market or a battle is a gain

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a prisoner walking towards the warders. The wordplay wants 'advances' as a plural noun and 'guards' as an instruction rather than a job.
explanation.definitionFit: Con → AGAINST: in 'the pros and cons' the con side is the one opposing, from the Latin contra, so the two words vote the same way.

clue.text: Annoying fly around light's in a muddle

indicators.note: Turning a thing around leaves it facing the way it came from, so those letters are read from the back.

parts.note: the annoying fly is a gnat, and it arrives here facing the other way
the LED is the light inside a modern bulb or torch

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves hide behind one picture, an insect circling a lamp: the fly has to become a word and the lamp has to become the three letters stamped on it.
explanation.definitionFit: in a muddle → TANGLED: hair or cable that is tangled has knotted itself into confusion, and being in a muddle is that state described from inside.

clue.text: Where plumber has spare part, hopefully installing one for nothing

indicators.note: To install a part is to fit it inside what is already there, so this letter drops into the middle instead of joining the end.

parts.words: Where plumber has spare part, hopefully
parts.note: a plumber's spare parts live in the van outside
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hopefully' earns its place: it is the setter admitting the part may not be there after all, which is exactly what makes the whole trip pointless.
explanation.definitionFit: for nothing → IN VAIN: work done in vain produces no result at all, and doing something for nothing is that same effort spent without reward.

clue.text: Victor and I love last minute break

parts.note: V is Victor in the radio alphabet
the letter standing for itself
love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as a zero
doing a thing at the last minute is doing it late

explanation.walkthrough: Three of the four pieces are single letters, which is what makes a clue like this feel harder than it is: 'Victor' and 'love' are both standing conventions.
explanation.definitionFit: break → VIOLATE: to violate a treaty, a rule or a curfew is to break it, the legal sense of the word rather than snapping something in two.

clue.text: Bit of glue inside sealing circular patch

indicators.note: A bit of a word is a fragment of it, and the smallest fragment on offer is the letter it opens with.
What goes inside sits within what is there already, so this letter drops into the join between the two words.

parts.note: an official seal is stamped onto the document
the opening letter of the word
circular means round

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is somebody gluing a patch on. 'Sealing' has to be heard as the stamping of a document before the fourteen letters will come apart.
explanation.definitionFit: patch → STAMPING GROUND: your stamping ground is the territory you habitually haunt, and 'patch' is the same idea in police and market-trader slang.

clue.text: Reel turning goes round

indicators.note: A thing that turns ends up facing the way it came from, so its letters are read from the far end.

parts.note: something that goes round loops, and those five letters turned about are the entry

explanation.walkthrough: A five-letter reversal has nowhere to hide, so the setter leans on 'Reel' and 'goes round' looking like the same idea - which they very nearly are.
explanation.definitionFit: Reel → SPOOL: both name the cylinder that thread, film or fishing line is wound onto, so this is a plain synonym in its equipment sense.

clue.text: Ruin unearthed entirely by Spooner

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of two words, so say the pair aloud and trade the sounds they start with.

parts.note: to unearth something is to find it, and entirely is all
trade the opening sounds of those two words and the same run of sound re-divides into one

explanation.walkthrough: Say 'found all' and the answer one after the other: it is the same string of sounds cut in a different place, which is what Spooner's trick always comes down to.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruin → DOWNFALL: a downfall is the collapse of a person's fortunes or standing, so it is ruin used of a career rather than of a building.

clue.text: Wooden hut guy occupied for period without power

indicators.note: Here 'without' means lacking rather than outside, so what it names is missing from the letters you have built.

parts.note: a guy is a chap
a flat let for a fortnight is occupied by whoever took it
P is the physics symbol for power, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The trick is seeing that the two pieces make a word of their own before anything is removed - a chaplet is a wreath or a rosary - and that is where the letter hides.
explanation.definitionFit: Wooden hut → CHALET: a chalet is the timber cabin of Swiss hillsides and English holiday camps, so 'wooden hut' plainly describes one.

clue.text: Clubs then set up for speaking informally

indicators.note: In a down clue something set up stands on its end, so its letters climb back the way they came.

parts.note: C is the card suit clubs
'then' gives SO, and this is SO stood on its end

explanation.walkthrough: Three letters, three jobs: a card suit, a turn-around and a conjunction almost nobody writes down. 'Speaking informally' is the setter flagging the casual spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: for speaking informally → COS: 'cos is the casual clipping of 'because', and the conjunction 'for' carries that same because-sense in careful English.

clue.text: Happy using high explosive for bombing campaign's finale

indicators.note: 'For' here means in place of, so the piece before it stands where the piece after it used to be.
A finale is the closing turn of a show, so it points at the last letter of the word it belongs to.

parts.note: the Blitz was Germany's bombing campaign against Britain in 1940
the last letter of that word, and the one being displaced
HE is the services' abbreviation for high explosive

explanation.walkthrough: A swap like this is rarer than a charade and reads like one until you notice 'for'. The surface never leaves the war, which is what hides the substitution.
explanation.definitionFit: Happy → BLITHE: blithe means light-heartedly cheerful, the carefree end of happy - as in a blithe spirit, untroubled by what is coming.

clue.text: Mess left after meal the day before

indicators.note: What comes after something stands behind it, so this letter is pushed to the end of the build.

parts.note: a dish is a meal, or the plate it arrives on
the eve of an event is the day before it
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads back to front: the single letter the sentence puts first is the one the answer puts last, which is exactly what 'after' is telling you.
explanation.definitionFit: Mess → DISHEVEL: to dishevel hair or clothing is to throw it into disorder, so 'mess' is the verb in its 'mess up' sense, not the noun.
